s01.text: Your CAPTCHA is hard because you are not passing a test. You are working for something bigger.

s02.text: The original reCAPTCHA, built by Luis von Ahn at Carnegie Mellon and acquired by Google in September 2009, was explicitly dual purpose: block the bots and use the answers to digitize text OCR could not read.

s03.text: A pair of words came back to you: a control word the system already knew, and an unknown word from a page the computer failed to read.

s04.text: Your job was to prove you are human. The second word was a side door: every time someone read a hard word, the system recorded that answer as evidence about what the scan said.

s05.text: By 2011 and 2012, the New York Times archive — back to 1851 — had been digitized this way, along with the older corpus from the New York Times request in 2007.

s06.text: In 2012 the system began mixing in photographs of house numbers taken from Google Street View.

s07.text: Google announced it was using the general public to read house numbers for its maps product.

s08.text: So what did you become? You became the labelling engine. The CAPTCHA verifies you; the words you read feed the machine.

s09.text: Why do captchas get harder over time? More pages are scanned, more words fail OCR, so the gap between easy and hard words grows — difficulty scales with how much labelling is still needed.

s10.text: That is the whole trick. The modern image-grid version behaves the same way: the pictures you categorize become training data for the next version of the system.

s11.text: Now the nuance, because it matters: we cannot prove that every individual puzzle you solved trained on your click — Google has never published what a specific challenge does.

s12.text: What the documented design and history show is dual purpose, from the primary sources.

s13.text: The difficulty scaling is the measurable claim we can make: difficulty tracks the amount of labelling still to be done, not how suspicious you look.

s14.text: A yellow warning: the street-view era was documented, but v2 and v3 came later and their internals are not published.

s15.text: One more honest note: CAPTCHA's impact is greatest for text-based challenges. The difficulty direction is stable.

s16.text: Sources: Wikipedia on reCAPTCHA; CMU News, September 2009; The New York Times, 2011; The Register, April 2012.

s17.text: Credits: Luis von Ahn, David Abraham, Manuel Blum, Colin McMillen, Ben Maurer, Edison Tan, Carnegie Mellon University.
